Unlike pointwise metrics such as [LPIPS Computation](5498-lpips-computation.md) which penalize phase shifts and exact pixel alignment, WD models human peripheral vision by aggregating features over local pooling regions, making it suitable for optimizing perceptual texture quality in differentiable rendering [S1][S2, unofficial].

The claim is fully supported by the provided evidence. Source [S1] explicitly states that pointwise metrics like LPIPS fail to account for texture perception (e.g., phase shifts) and that WD addresses this by aggregating over local regions, motivated by models of human peripheral vision encoding images using summary statistics. Source [S2] corroborates this by explaining that larger kernel sizes in WD mimic human peripheral vision by prioritizing neighborhood-level statistical alignment over point-wise fidelity, making it suitable for perceptual quality.
